title: Attribute Routing in ASP.NET Core
description: Use C# attributes on controllers and actions to define precise, RESTful URL routes.

data.text: Attribute routing lets you define routes directly on controllers and action methods using C# attributes. Instead of configuring all routes in `Program.cs`, each action declares its own URL pattern. This is the preferred approach for Web APIs and apps that need fine-grained control over URLs.

terms.definition: An attribute applied to a controller or action to define the URL pattern it handles.
HTTP method attributes that restrict an action to a specific verb.
A placeholder in a route template like {id} that captures part of the URL.
A rule that limits what values a parameter can match, like {id:int}.

data.caption: Attribute routing maps URL templates directly to controller actions.

data.title: Quick Check
data.text: Use `MapControllers()` for attribute routing and `MapControllerRoute()` for convention-based routing. You can use both in the same app if needed.
Apply the `[Route]` attribute at the controller level to set a base URL prefix. Then add additional `[Route]` or HTTP-method attributes on individual actions:

data.text: The `[controller]` token is replaced by the controller name without the `Controller` suffix — so `ProductsController` becomes `api/products`. This keeps routes in sync with the class name automatically.

data.text: Attribute routes support the same parameter placeholders as convention-based routes. ASP.NET Core also provides special tokens that are replaced automatically:

items: `[controller]` — replaced by the controller class name without the `Controller` suffix.
`[action]` — replaced by the action method name.
`{id?}` — an optional parameter (the `?` makes it optional).

data.description: Create a TasksController with attribute routing that supports GET /api/tasks, GET /api/tasks/{id}, POST /api/tasks, and DELETE /api/tasks/{id}. Use a simple in-memory list. Add route constraints to ensure the id is always an integer.
steps: Create a Task model with Id, Title, and IsComplete properties.
Add GetAll, GetById, Create, and Delete actions with correct HTTP attributes.
Add a route constraint to the id parameter.
Test each endpoint in the browser or with curl.
data.expectedOutcome: You will understand how to define clean RESTful routes using attributes and how route constraints protect your endpoints.

items.text: Call app.MapControllers() in Program.cs to enable attribute routing.
items.hint: MapControllers is for attribute routes only.

items.text: Use [controller] and [action] tokens to keep routes maintainable.
items.hint: Tokens auto-update if you rename the class or method.

items.text: Use [HttpGet], [HttpPost], etc. to restrict actions to specific verbs.
items.hint: This prevents accidental access via the wrong HTTP method.

items.text: Add route constraints like {id:int} for safer parameter matching.
items.hint: Constraints return 404 instead of calling the wrong action.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Attribute routing defines routes directly on controllers and actions using [Route].
Use MapControllers() in Program.cs to enable attribute routing.
[controller] and [action] tokens keep routes in sync with class and method names.
HTTP method attributes like [HttpGet] and [HttpPost] restrict which verbs an action accepts.
Route constraints like {id:int} make routes safer and more precise.
data.takeaway: Attribute routing gives you precise control over every URL in your app. It is the standard approach for building RESTful APIs in ASP.NET Core.
